probes.query: An operator has built database files ahead of time and moves them into a cluster that is already running and has several server groups. While the move runs, ordinary client requests get turned away. Trace what puts the servers into that turning-away state, how the change spreads to every replica of every group, and how a replica that was absent during the move ends up with the data afterwards.
expectedFacts: The import client (initiateSnapshotStream in dgraph/cmd/dgraphimport/import_client.go) first sends a Start request to the edgraph server handler Server.UpdateExtSnapshotStreamingState, which checks admin authorization and calls worker.ProposeDrain.

ProposeDrain (worker/import.go) reaches the leader of every group (locally when this node leads the group) and grpcWorker.UpdateExtSnapshotStreamingState there proposes an ExtSnapshotState proposal through Raft.

CRITICAL: When each replica applies that proposal in node.applyCommitted (worker/draft.go), the Start case calls x.ExtSnapshotStreamingState(true), which sets both the import flag and the draining flag, so x.HealthCheck (x/health.go) returns the draining-mode error to ordinary requests.

CRITICAL: On the Finish proposal, a replica whose import flag is still set (it did not itself receive the stream, since the stream handlers clear the flag when they end) asks its group leader for a snapshot via populateSnapshot and then runs postStreamProcessing.
The data is streamed group by group (streamSnapshot -> StreamExtSnapshot -> worker.InStream / streamInGroup), where the receiving group leader forwards the stream to its followers.

probes.query: When a filter checks that a field is the same as some value, among a given list of candidate nodes, the server sometimes skips the field's search index and instead reads each candidate's own stored value. expectedFacts: CRITICAL: handleUidPostings (worker/task.go) records, for every index key read by a comparison function, the approximate length of that index list with posting.GetStatsHolder().InsertRecord(attr, token, size).
posting/stats.go keeps a StatsHolder with one EqContainer per predicate; each container wraps a count-min sketch (algo.NewCountMinSketch) that estimates how many nodes share a token.
The StatsHolder is created in initMemoryLayer (posting/mvcc.go) and hangs off the MemoryLayer singleton, reachable through GetStatsHolder().

planForEqFilter (worker/task.go) keeps using the index if any candidate uid is 0, and reads values directly if the candidate list is shorter than the configured type-filter limit (Config.TypeFilterUidLimit, default 10).

CRITICAL: Otherwise it sums ProcessEqPredicate estimates for the eq tokens and reads values directly only when the candidate count is below estimate divided by that limit; the first lookup for a predicate has no estimate (returns max uint64 and creates the container), so the index is used.

mergeMapShardsIntoReduceShards (merge_shards.go) moves map shard 0 into reduce shard 0 (so reserved predicates land in group 1) and then places the remaining map shards, largest first, into the currently smallest reduce shard.
The bulk run.go creates one output directory per reduce shard and writes a group_id file containing index+1 into each output p directory (x.WriteGroupIdFile).

probes.query: A schema author wants an external scripting service to hear about every successful write to one data type. Trace how this is declared, how the server decides to notify for a given write, where the destination address comes from, and what happens when delivery fails.
expectedFacts: The notification is declared with the @lambdaOnMutate directive (add/update/delete arguments) on a type (graphql/schema/gqlschema.go); lambdaOnMutateValidation (graphql/schema/rules.go) rejects it unless the alpha was started with a graphql lambda-url and rejects it on @remote types.

lambdaOnMutateMappings (graphql/schema/wrappers.go) builds a map keyed by argument name plus type name (for example add + Person) for every argument set to true; mutation.HasLambdaOnMutate looks up the mutation's own name in that map.

CRITICAL: In graphql/resolve/mutation.go the decision is made only after the transaction has committed; if HasLambdaOnMutate holds, sendWebhookEvent runs in a separate goroutine with the commit timestamp and the root uids.

sendWebhookEvent (graphql/resolve/webhook.go) POSTs a JSON payload (event with typename, operation, commit timestamp and add/update/delete data, plus the caller's access token) to x.LambdaUrl(ns), which substitutes the namespace id for $ns in the configured lambda-url.
CRITICAL: Delivery is best effort: errors and non-2xx statuses are only logged at verbosity 3; there is no retry and nothing is returned to the GraphQL caller.

probes.query: Some part of the cluster evens out stored data between groups, so it must know how large each field's stored data is on every group. Trace how those sizes are measured, delivered to the coordinator, kept only when worth keeping, and then used to pick what to move.
expectedFacts: node.processTabletSizes (worker/draft.go) runs calculateTabletSizes on a fixed 5-minute tick, and only the group leader does the work.

CRITICAL: calculateTabletSizes adds up on-disk and uncompressed sizes of Badger tables per predicate, counting only tables whose first and last key belong to the same predicate, and sends them with groupi.doSendMembership (worker/groups.go), which attaches tablets only when the sender is the group leader.

CRITICAL: Zero's UpdateMembership (dgraph/cmd/zero/zero.go) calls createProposals, which ignores tablet data from non-leaders and proposes a tablet update only when the tablet is removed, goes from size 0 to non-zero, or its on-disk size changed by more than 10 percent.

Server.chooseTablet (dgraph/cmd/zero/tablet.go), run on the rebalance interval by the Zero leader, ranks groups by summed OnDiskBytes and, starting from the largest, tries to move from a source group to the smallest group, skipping a source whose gap to the smallest is under 10 percent of the smallest group's size (or that has no suitable tablet) and trying the next largest.
chooseTablet picks the largest non-reserved tablet whose size is at most half the gap and that is not in failure backoff.

probes.query: Besides a client choosing to roll back, list the different situations in which the cluster itself forces a transaction to fail or disappear, and say where each is decided. Count only decisions made by server code, across both the coordinator and the data servers.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: The coordinator's commit-time conflict check (Oracle.hasConflict, used by Server.commit in dgraph/cmd/zero/oracle.go) aborts a transaction that began before the current leader took over or whose written keys were committed later by someone else.

CRITICAL: Server.commit also aborts when a touched predicate is unknown, now served by a different group than the one that wrote it, or has commits blocked because it is being moved (checkPreds in dgraph/cmd/zero/oracle.go).

The group leader runs abortOldTransactions every minute (checkpointAndClose in worker/draft.go), which asks Zero (blockingAbort -> TryAbort) to abort transactions whose last write is older than the idle limit, then proposes only the aborts.

Before a schema change or a predicate drop is applied, detectPendingTxns (worker/draft.go) finds transactions with pending writes on that predicate, returns a retry error and launches tryAbortTransactions (worker/mutation.go).

Drop-all, drop-data and namespace-drop operations discard pending transactions without a verdict by clearing the posting oracle's pending map (ResetTxns / ResetTxnsForNs in posting/oracle.go, called from applyMutations in worker/draft.go).

probes.query: A team lets each dependency be fetched either as an archive or as a version-control checkout. They choose per package-name pattern, with a catch-all entry, in both their user-level and their project-level settings. Trace how those two layers of settings are combined, how the resulting patterns reach the component that fetches packages, how that component picks the first origin to try for a package that tracks a development branch, and what happens when that first origin fails. Include how an explicit command-line preference interacts with the patterns.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: Config::merge handles the preferred-install key specially: a plain string value is turned into a map with the catch-all pattern, new values are combined with array_merge (patterns already present keep their position, new patterns from the later layer are appended after the earlier layer's patterns), and the catch-all entry is moved to the end so it is matched last.

Factory::createDownloadManager calls DownloadManager::setPreferences only when the configured value is an array; when it is the plain string 'dist' or 'source' it sets the prefer-dist or prefer-source flag instead.

DownloadManager::resolvePackageInstallPreference walks the pattern map in order, turns '*' into a case-insensitive anchored regex wildcard, and the first match wins: 'dist' gives dist, 'auto' gives dist for stable packages and source for dev packages, anything else gives source; with no match a dev package gets source and a stable package gets dist.

CRITICAL: DownloadManager::getAvailableSources lists source before dist by default and reverses to dist-first only when prefer-source is false and (prefer-dist is true or the pattern result is dist); on updates it keeps the previously installed package's source if the new package offers it, except when a stable dist install is replaced by a dev version.

Command-line choices reach the manager through BaseCommand::getPreferredInstallOptions and Installer::run, which calls setPreferSource and setPreferDist on the DownloadManager before downloading, so an explicit flag takes priority over the pattern map.

DownloadManager::download retries with the next origin only when the next origin is 'dist' (a source failure may fall back to dist); a dist failure is rethrown without falling back to source, and an IrrecoverableDownloadException is never retried.

probes.query: When a dependency update is set to refuse versions with known vulnerabilities, the first request for vulnerability data asks for a reduced form of each record. expectedFacts: SecurityAdvisoryPoolFilter::filter first calls RepositorySet::getMatchingSecurityAdvisories with partial records allowed, for pool packages that are not root, not platform and not locked, passing the blocking ignore list and the update-scope ignore-unreachable setting.

RepositorySet::getMatchingSecurityAdvisories builds one OR-constraint of exact versions per package name (skipping root aliases and unversioned dev branches) and RepositorySet::getSecurityAdvisoriesForConstraints asks each repository that provides advisories; a TransportException is rethrown unless unreachable repositories are ignored, in which case the repository is recorded.

ComposerRepository::getSecurityAdvisories reads advisories embedded in per-package metadata when the repository advertises metadata and (partial records are allowed or no API URL exists); names not answered that way are sent to the advisory API URL by POST in batches of 500 with a 10 second timeout.

PartialSecurityAdvisory::create returns a full SecurityAdvisory only when title, sources and reportedAt are present, otherwise a partial record with only ID, package and affected versions; ComposerRepository throws a RuntimeException if a partial record arrives when full records were requested.

CRITICAL: Auditor::needsCompleteAdvisoryLoad returns true only when at least one advisory is partial AND at least one key of the blocking ignore list does not start with 'PKSA-' (so CVE or remote IDs, and also ignored package names, need full data); then SecurityAdvisoryPoolFilter::filter repeats the lookup with partial records disallowed.
AdvisoriesPolicyConfig::getIgnoreListForOperation supplies that ignore list, merging ignored advisory IDs with ignored package names for the 'block' operation.

probes.query: After a login, application code asks the framework to issue a brand-new session identifier for the same visitor. If the session needs a change it calls SessionManager::changeSessionId, then adds a session cookie with the new identifier (path '/', configured SameSite, max-age only when it is >= 0) to that response, using a temporary copy when the response is a shared cached object (HttpAppFrameworkImpl.cc:728-770).

(SessionManager.cc:116-127; CacheMap.h:217-247).

probes.query: A caller's Swift task gets cancelled while an async database access is in the middle of a long-running query. By what route does the cancellation reach SQLite, and why does the caller end up with a task-cancellation error instead of a database error? Cover the whole path from the cancellation signal to the thrown error.
expectedFacts: SerializedDatabase.execute (the async variant) wraps the access in withTaskCancellationHandler; inside the access it stores db.cancel in a mutex-guarded slot, and the onCancel handler calls that closure (SerializedDatabase.swift:253-270).

CRITICAL: Database.cancel sets Suspension.isCancelled and, when interruptsWhenCancelled is true, calls sqlite3_interrupt on the connection, which makes the running statement stop (Database.swift:1245-1268).
Statement stepping (executeAllSteps, forEachStep, step) sends any step result other than ROW/DONE to Database.statementDidFail (Statement.swift:566-623).

CRITICAL: For SQLITE_INTERRUPT or SQLITE_ABORT, Database.statementDidFail calls suspensionMutex.load().checkCancellation(), which throws CancellationError when the access is cancelled and interruptsWhenCancelled is true, before any DatabaseError is built (Database+Statements.swift:497-503; Database.swift:370-374).

A statement that starts after the cancellation never runs: statementWillExecute calls checkForSuspensionViolation, which tests the cancelled flag before the suspended flag and throws CancellationError (Database+Statements.swift:449; Database.swift:1388-1393, 1427-1428).

When the access ends, its defer block clears the state with db.uncancel(); DatabasePool.barrierWriteWithoutTransaction (async) repeats the same pattern (SerializedDatabase.swift:258-262; DatabasePool.swift:812-830).

probes.query: A listener registered on a write connection refuses a transaction by throwing from its before-commit callback. Trace how that refusal turns into a rollback inside SQLite, which error the code that issued the commit finally sees, and what the other registered listeners are told afterwards.
expectedFacts: Database.setUp installs the commit and rollback hooks through observationBroker?.installCommitAndRollbackHooks(); read-only connections have no broker (Database.swift:471-474, 516).

CRITICAL: The sqlite3_commit_hook callback calls broker.databaseWillCommit(), which calls databaseWillCommit on every observer; if one throws, the hook stores transactionCompletion = .cancelledCommit(error) and returns 1, so SQLite turns the COMMIT into a rollback (TransactionObserver.swift:494-501, 664-679).
The sqlite3_rollback_hook callback keeps .cancelledCommit as it is; for any other completion it records .rollback (TransactionObserver.swift:681-692).

The failed COMMIT step reaches Statement's step loop as an error code, which calls Database.statementDidFail; that method calls observationBroker.statementDidFail before it builds any DatabaseError (Statement.swift:566-580; Database+Statements.swift:474-496).

CRITICAL: DatabaseObservationBroker.statementDidFail, on .cancelledCommit(error), runs databaseDidRollback(notifyTransactionObservers: !isReadOnly) and then rethrows that same error, so the committing caller sees the observer's own error and not a SQLite constraint error (TransactionObserver.swift:354-373).

databaseDidRollback sends databaseDidRollback to every registered observer (including the one that threw) inside ignoringCancellation, then databaseDidEndTransaction drops observers whose extent was the next transaction and re-enables the others (TransactionObserver.swift:571-600).

probes.query: An application declares that one record type 'owns many' records of another type without naming any columns, then asks for a join from the owner to its children. Follow the path from that declaration to the join condition in the generated SQL: where does the code learn which columns to use, which table's column ends up on which side of the equality, and what happens if the child table declares two references to the owner?
expectedFacts: HasManyAssociation.init builds an SQLForeignKeyCondition with the optional user ForeignKey and originIsLeft: false (the child table holds the reference); BelongsToAssociation uses true (HasManyAssociation.swift:70-73; BelongsToAssociation.swift:71-74).

SQLQualifiedJoin.sql writes 'JOIN <table> ON ...' by calling condition.joinExpression(db, leftAlias:, rightAlias:) (SQLQueryGenerator.swift:786-835, call at :824), which for a foreign-key condition calls foreignKey.joinMapping(db, from: leftAlias.tableName) (SQLRelation.swift:834-847).

CRITICAL: SQLForeignKeyCondition.foreignKeyRequest swaps origin and destination tables when originIsLeft is false, and SQLForeignKeyRequest.fetchForeignKeyMapping resolves the columns: use the user columns when complete; otherwise filter Database.foreignKeys(on: originTable) by destination table; if none match and origin columns are known, pair them with the destination table's primary key (SQLRelation.swift:894-914; SQLForeignKeyRequest.swift:24-115).

CRITICAL: When more than one schema foreign key from the child to the owner matches, the code does not throw: it calls fatalError telling the user to provide an explicit ForeignKey (SQLForeignKeyRequest.swift:78-90).

ForeignKeyMapping.joinMapping(originIsLeft:) orients the pairs: with originIsLeft false the owner's destination column is on the left and the child's origin column on the right (SQLForeignKeyRequest.swift:170-176).
JoinMapping.joinExpression(leftAlias:rightAlias:) renders 'right.column = left.column' for each pair joined with AND, giving ON child.ownerId = owner.id (SQLRelation.swift:1004-1006).

probes.query: A multi-reader database is observed for changes to a query result. The first value must arrive quickly even while a long write is running, yet no change that lands between that first read and the start of listening may be missed. Explain the mechanism step by step, and say what the code falls back to on builds or files where the needed SQLite version-comparison feature is unavailable.
expectedFacts: DatabasePool._add sends a plain observation of a writable pool to _addConcurrent, which creates a ValueConcurrentObserver whose start() reads the initial value from a reader instead of waiting for the writer (DatabasePool.swift:732-777; ValueConcurrentObserver.swift:234-277).

CRITICAL: With snapshot support, the initial read runs inside a long-lived WALSnapshotTransaction obtained from DatabasePool.walSnapshotTransaction: a deferred read transaction on a reader that also records a WALSnapshot of that moment (WALSnapshotTransaction.swift:66-86; DatabasePool.swift:689-701).

CRITICAL: asyncStartObservation then runs on the writer queue, takes a WALSnapshot of the writer connection and compares it with the initial one (sqlite3_snapshot_cmp via WALSnapshot.compare); if the writer's is newer, or the writer's snapshot cannot be taken, it assumes a change, fetches again from the writer and notifies a fresh value; otherwise it only starts observing (ValueConcurrentObserver.swift:423-520, comparison at :451-460; WALSnapshot.swift:89-91).
The snapshot transaction is closed right after the comparison so that its reader returns to the pool (ValueConcurrentObserver.swift:464).

Without snapshot support (compiled without SQLITE_ENABLE_SNAPSHOT or with SQLITE_DISABLE_SNAPSHOT, which Package.swift defines on Linux) the #else branch sends syncStart and asyncStart to the WithoutWALSnapshot variants, which always fetch a second time from the writer after observation starts, so the same value can be notified twice (ValueConcurrentObserver.swift:279, 527-537, 543-700; Package.swift:17-19).

At run time, if the snapshot cannot be created (SQLITE_ERROR: missing or empty WAL file) the observer degrades to the same without-snapshot path; Database.setUpWALMode therefore creates and drops a small table to guarantee a non-empty WAL file (ValueConcurrentObserver.swift:296-300, 411-418; Database.swift:531-562).

probes.query: While SQLite compiles each SQL statement, GRDB learns several kinds of facts about it through SQLite's permission-check callback. List each kind of fact the library keeps for a statement, and for each name the component that later uses it and what it uses it for.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: Read access (SQLITE_READ) builds selectedRegion, stored as Statement.databaseRegion; it records what a statement reads: Database.statementWillExecute passes it to registerAccess(to:), which feeds the region that ValueObservation records while fetching, and FetchRequest.databaseRegion(_:) returns it when a request is used as an observed region (either consumer is acceptable) (StatementAuthorizer.swift:115-125; Statement.swift:162; Database+Statements.swift:452; Database.swift:934-937; FetchRequest.swift:104).

CRITICAL: Write effects (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, including trigger and foreign-key-action effects) build databaseEventKinds, stored as Statement.authorizerEventKinds; TransactionObservation.statementObservation(for:) uses them to decide which observers, and which events, are activated for the statement, and canDeleteRows makes Database.add/remove(transactionObserver:) evict cached statements that delete (StatementAuthorizer.swift:127-161; TransactionObserver.swift:44-45, 66-67, 1045-1090).

The schema-changing flag (DROP, CREATE, ALTER, ATTACH, DETACH, and the sqlite_drop_column function before SQLite 3.38) becomes Statement.invalidatesDatabaseSchemaCache; Database.statementDidExecute then clears the schema cache (StatementAuthorizer.swift:98-113, 186-203; Database+Statements.swift:461-464).

The transaction or savepoint effect becomes Statement.transactionEffect: DatabaseObservationBroker.statementDidExecute uses it to maintain the savepoint stack and to detect empty transactions, checkForSuspensionViolation lets rollbacks and read-only commits through, and Statement.releasesDatabaseLock builds on it (StatementAuthorizer.swift:163-185; TransactionObserver.swift:389-430; Database.swift:1367-1374; Statement.swift:808-824).

The query-only pragma flag becomes Statement.isQueryOnlyPragma, which checkForSuspensionViolation uses to let that pragma run even when the database is suspended (StatementAuthorizer.swift:204-207; Database.swift:1378-1380).

Besides recording, the callback returns SQLITE_IGNORE for DELETE on tables whose deletions some observer watches, which disables SQLite's truncate optimization so individual row deletions reach the update hook (StatementAuthorizer.swift:132-155).

probes.query: Some cleanup steps in the library must still work when the current database access has been cancelled or the connection interrupted; otherwise the connection could be left in a bad state. Which places make that guarantee, and how does each one do it?
expectedFacts: Database.endReadOnly runs the statement that leaves read-only mode inside ignoringInterruption, so an interruption cannot leave the connection permanently unable to write (Database.swift:844-860).

CRITICAL: Database.rollback runs ROLLBACK inside ignoringInterruption, so an interruption cannot leave a transaction open (which would trip the unsafe-transaction precondition); ignoringInterruption retries the closure once after CancellationError, SQLITE_INTERRUPT or SQLITE_ABORT and resets all prepared statements first (Database.swift:1297-1313, 1782-1795).

CRITICAL: DatabaseObservationBroker.databaseDidCommit and databaseDidRollback notify transaction observers inside Database.ignoringCancellation, so observers can still use the database even if the committing task was cancelled (TransactionObserver.swift:504-515, 571-587; Database.swift:1279-1292).
Database.checkForSuspensionViolation never blocks rollbacks, commits on a read-only connection, or the query-only pragma, even when the database is cancelled or suspended (Database.swift:1355-1380).

Read accesses finish with 'try commit, else try rollback' so the read-only transaction is always left even if commit fails with CancellationError: DatabasePool async read, asyncRead and asyncConcurrentRead, DatabaseQueue.asyncRead and spawnConcurrentRead, DatabaseSnapshot.deinit and WALSnapshotTransaction.commitAndRelease (DatabasePool.swift:362-372, 392-405, 563-571; DatabaseQueue.swift:249-258, 303-312; DatabaseSnapshot.swift:112-123; WALSnapshotTransaction.swift:13-27).

probes.query: In a database with several reader connections, what makes sure a reader never goes back into the pool of reusable readers while it is still inside an open read transaction, or else is thrown away instead of reused? Name each safeguard and where it lives.
expectedFacts: DatabasePool.init forces allowsUnsafeTransactions = false on the reader configuration, whatever the user configured, because the same reader may not be obtained again to close a dangling transaction (DatabasePool.swift:56-63; Configuration.swift:278-282).

CRITICAL: SerializedDatabase.preconditionNoUnsafeTransactionLeft is a fatal precondition run (via defer) at the end of sync, reentrantSync, async and async execute accesses; it fails if the connection is still inside a transaction, unless an override or the configuration allows it (SerializedDatabase.swift:131, 142, 197-234, 261, 297-309).

Synchronous DatabasePool.read runs the user closure inside Database.isolated, which opens a savepoint (a real transaction when outermost) and commits it when the closure returns (DatabasePool.swift:339-352; Database.swift:1569-1597).
The async read paths begin a deferred transaction and use a defer that tries commit and falls back to rollback before the reader is released with .reuse (DatabasePool.swift:354-379, 381-415).

CRITICAL: For long-lived snapshot reads, walSnapshotTransaction and asyncWALSnapshotTransaction release the reader with .discard instead of .reuse when it is still inside a transaction, and WALSnapshotTransaction.commitAndRelease tries hard to leave the transaction first; Pool.release removes a discarded reader from the pool (DatabasePool.swift:694-700, 716-723; WALSnapshotTransaction.swift:13-27; Pool.swift:165-175).

probes.query: Two full-text virtual table integrations can keep their index in step with an ordinary table by means of triggers. A maintainer wants to remove the automatic upkeep for the variant whose upkeep uses only after-event triggers (no before-event ones). Which public helper removes it, which trigger names does it drop, where are those triggers created and at what moment of the table-creation flow, and what runs right after they are created?
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: The helper is Database.dropFTS5SynchronizationTriggers(forTable:); it drops the three triggers named __<table>_ai, __<table>_ad and __<table>_au (FTS5.swift:536-541).

CRITICAL: Those triggers are created by FTS5.database(_:didCreate:using:) when the definition is synchronized with a content table (set by FTS5TableDefinition.synchronize(withTable:)); all three are AFTER INSERT, AFTER DELETE and AFTER UPDATE triggers, and delete or update remove old entries by inserting a row with the special 'delete' command into the index table (FTS5.swift:226-280, 472-474).

Database.create(virtualTable:...) runs CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE and then calls module.database(_:didCreate:using:), both inside inSavepoint, so the triggers appear in the same atomic step as the table (VirtualTableModule.swift:182-187).

Right after the triggers, the code runs the 'rebuild' command on the index table so already existing content rows are indexed; temporary external-content tables are refused with a fatal error (FTS5.swift:232-241, 281).

The other variant's helper, dropFTS4SynchronizationTriggers, drops four triggers (__<table>_bu, _bd, _au, _ai: two BEFORE and two AFTER) and deletes old entries with a plain DELETE by docid, so it is not the one asked about (FTS4.swift:136-153, 404-410).

probes.query: A multi-reader database is observed using the default, most flexible observation style, where the set of tables read by the fetch closure can change from one run to the next. When a write transaction commits, which connection runs the re-fetch, and why? Which other observation style lets the re-fetch run on a reader connection, and which observer class handles the cases where the observation is placed on a single-connection database or is flagged as needing write access?
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: The default tracking(_:) style sets trackingMode .nonConstantRegionRecordedFromSelection; in ValueConcurrentObserver.databaseDidCommit that mode fetches from the writer connection (fetchRecordingObservedRegion(writerDB)) and updates the tracked region (ValueObservation.swift:986-993; ValueConcurrentObserver.swift:759-787).

The reason is that after a concurrent reader fetch has its snapshot, a change could land in the next tracked region, which was not known yet, so a change would be missed; with a non-constant region the fetch must run on the writer (comment at ValueConcurrentObserver.swift:759-773).

CRITICAL: trackingConstantRegion(_:) (.constantRegionRecordedFromSelection) and tracking(regions:fetch:) (.constantRegion) take the other branch: setNeedsFetching coalesces requests with a FetchingState (idle, fetching, fetchingAndNeedsFetch) and asyncFetch runs the fetch on a pool reader through dbPool.asyncRead (ValueObservation.swift:786-793, 928-936; ValueConcurrentObserver.swift:756-758, 791-833).

DatabasePool._add picks the observer: a read-only pool uses _addReadOnly, an observation with requiresWriteAccess uses _addWriteOnly, otherwise _addConcurrent builds the ValueConcurrentObserver (DatabasePool.swift:732-777).

A DatabaseQueue (or any DatabaseWriter other than a pool, or a pool observation flagged as needing writes) goes through DatabaseWriter._addWriteOnly, which creates a ValueWriteOnlyObserver that always fetches from the writer connection in databaseDidCommit (DatabaseQueue.swift:331-348; DatabaseWriter.swift:588-607; ValueWriteOnlyObserver.swift:366-420).

probes.query: A record type has a property that is a list of small structs, and each struct holds a point in time. When the record is written to the database, in what form does that time end up in the stored text, and which piece of code chooses that form? How does it differ from a point-in-time property declared directly on the record?
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: RecordEncoder.encode(_:forKey:) first tries a single-value ColumnEncoder; when the value encodes into a keyed or unkeyed container (as an array of structs does), ColumnEncoder sets requiresJSON, a JSONRequiredError is thrown, and the value is encoded again as JSON (EncodableRecord+Encodable.swift:119-166, 244-275).

CRITICAL: The JSON is produced with Record.databaseJSONEncoder(for: key); its default dateEncodingStrategy is .millisecondsSince1970, so the nested time is stored as a number of milliseconds since 1970 (also base64 data, sorted keys, non-finite floats throw) (EncodableRecord.swift:236-247).
The JSON bytes are turned into a String and persisted as the column value (EncodableRecord+Encodable.swift:159-160).

A Date property declared directly on the record bypasses the JSON encoder: it goes through databaseDateEncodingStrategy(for:), whose default .deferredToDate uses Date's DatabaseValueConvertible text 'yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss.SSS' in UTC (EncodableRecord+Encodable.swift:125-128; EncodableRecord.swift:253-257; Date.swift:155-160).

Look-alikes that are not used here: DatabaseValueConvertible.databaseJSONEncoder() (same defaults, only for values that are both DatabaseValueConvertible and Encodable) and JSONDumpFormat.defaultEncoder (debug dump output) (DatabaseValueConvertible.swift:118-126; DatabaseValueConvertible+Encodable.swift:142; JSONDumpFormat.swift:55-65).

probes.query: A developer backs a record type with an SQL view. Saving or finding by key fails because the library says the view has no key. How can the application tell the library which columns identify a row of a view, where is that information consulted, what happens when several such providers are combined, and in which situation is it deliberately switched off?
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: The application sets Configuration.schemaSource to a DatabaseSchemaSource implementing columnsForPrimaryKey(_:inView:); each connection copies it in Database.init (Configuration.swift:441; Database.swift:467).

CRITICAL: The private Database.primaryKey(_:) first checks, when a schemaSource exists and the name is a view, schemaSource.columnsForPrimaryKey, and turns the columns into key info with fetchPrimitivePrimaryKey(forView:columns:) (a regular key, tableHasRowID false); otherwise it falls back to table introspection, which for a view leads to the 'database view has no primary key' error (Database+Schema.swift:415-437, 534-566, 372-376).
Several sources are combined with then(_:) into Chained2SchemaSource: the first source returning non-nil wins, results are never merged (DatabaseSchemaSource.swift:195-216).

Migration.run executes every migration inside db.withSchemaSource(nil), so migrations see the raw SQLite schema; withSchemaSource swaps the source and clears the schema cache before and after the block (Migration.swift:29-33; Database+Schema.swift:42-57).
The source also affects unique-key lookups: columnsForUniqueKey calls primaryKey(_:), so the columns a source returns for a view count as a unique key of that view (Database+Schema.swift:1101-1121).

probes.query: A developer registers schema-change steps using the default referential-integrity setting. One step is registered, then the migrator is switched to its unsafe, faster mode, then a second step is registered. For each of the two steps, on a connection that has referential constraints turned on and on a connection that has them turned off, what does the library run before, during and after the step?
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: The migrator's option is read when a step is registered, not when it runs: registerMigration maps .deferred to Migration.ForeignKeyChecks.deferred if defersForeignKeyChecks is still true, and to .disabled otherwise; the earlier step keeps .deferred, the later step gets .disabled (DatabaseMigrator.swift:157-159, 319-340).

CRITICAL: On a connection with foreign keys ON, the earlier (deferred) step runs with foreign_keys switched OFF, inside an immediate transaction; after the step and the bookkeeping insert, db.checkForeignKeys() verifies the data before COMMIT, and foreign_keys is switched back ON in a finally block (Migration.swift:34-37, 79-109).

On a connection with foreign keys ON, the later (disabled) step runs the same way (foreign_keys OFF, immediate transaction, ON again in finally) but with no checkForeignKeys call, so violations are not detected (Migration.swift:64-77).

On a connection with foreign keys OFF, Migration.run takes the else branch for both steps: an immediate transaction with the migration and the bookkeeping, no pragma changes and no check (Migration.swift:34, 43-45, 56-62).

A step registered with foreignKeyChecks .immediate always maps to .immediate, whatever the migrator option, and runs in an immediate transaction without toggling the pragma (DatabaseMigrator.swift:327-329; Migration.swift:56-62). All paths run inside db.withSchemaSource(nil) (Migration.swift:33).

probes.notes: VERIFICATION: DatabaseMigrator.swift:113 (defersForeignKeyChecks = true), :157-159 (disablingDeferredForeignKeyChecks returns a copy with the flag false; doc says 'newly registered migrations'), :312-342 (registerMigration: :321-326 deferred -> deferred|disabled by the flag captured now, :327-328 immediate -> immediate); Migration.swift:29-47 (run: PRAGMA foreign_keys query at :34; switch at :35-42; else immediate at :43-45), :56-62 (runWithImmediate), :64-77 (runWithDisabled), :79-109 (runWithDeferred: foreign_keys=OFF :85, inTransaction(.immediate) :89, checkForeignKeys :98, ON in finally :107). CHEAPEST ROUTE (5 dependent steps): (1) grep 'foreign key' + 'migrat' -> DatabaseMigrator.swift and Migration.swift; (2) read DatabaseMigrator.registerMigration for the mapping; (3) notice the flag is read at registration, order matters; (4) read Migration.run for the pragma branch; (5) read the three runWith* bodies to state before/during/after for each. The question avoids 'foreign key', 'deferred', 'disabling', but 'migrator' reaches the gold file at grep 1 (acknowledged); the order-of-registration trap and the second layer (Migration.run) are what make it a 5-step question. probes.query: A record type stamps the time of the current write on each row it saves, using the library's notion of the time of the current transaction. Two inserts run inside one write block, another insert runs outside any explicit transaction, and in a third case the configured time source throws when the transaction begins. What timestamps do the inserts see, at what moment is the time captured, and when is the failure reported?
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: The time is captured once per transaction: checkForAutocommitTransition runs after each statement executes, and when the connection has just left autocommit mode (the BEGIN statement completed) it stores transactionDateResult = Result { try configuration.transactionClock.now(self) }; both inserts in the write block therefore read the same date (Database+Statements.swift:461-469, 537-553; Database.swift:424-437).

The captured time is the moment the transaction began, not the moment of the first insert; the stored result is cleared when the connection returns to autocommit mode (Database+Statements.swift:547-551).
Outside any transaction transactionDateResult is nil, so Database.transactionDate calls the clock again on every access and returns a fresh date each time (Database.swift:424-437).

CRITICAL: If the clock throws at transaction start, the error is stored inside the Result, BEGIN itself still succeeds, and the error is rethrown only when transactionDate is read, on every read for the rest of that transaction (Database+Statements.swift:541-545; Database.swift:432-434).

The default clock is DefaultTransactionClock, which simply returns Date() (not an SQLite time); Configuration.transactionClock can be replaced with .custom { db in ... } (TransactionClock.swift:44-52; Configuration.swift:200).
probes.author: r3hb-grdb-drafter
probes.notes: VERIFICATION: Database.swift:399 (autocommitState), :400-407 (transactionDateResult invariant), :424-437 (transactionDate getter: stored result else clock); Database+Statements.swift:461-469 (statementDidExecute -> checkForAutocommitTransition at :466), :474-495 (statementDidFail also calls it at :483), :537-553 (transition on -> off: captures Result; off -> on: nil); TransactionClock.swift:18-24, :44-52 (DefaultTransactionClock returns Date()), :55-64 (custom); Configuration.swift:191-200. FIRST 3 GREPS of the question's words: 'timestamp' (docs RecordTimestamps.md, tests), 'time of the transaction' (docs), 'clock' (TransactionClock.swift = gold). DECOYS: Date() calls elsewhere (DatabaseValue Date conversion), Documentation/RecordTimestamps.md (shows usage, does not state error timing), Database.beginTransaction, SQLite's own CURRENT_TIMESTAMP. est. turns: 6.

probes.query: An application sets, on the configuration shared by all its connections, how a connection should behave when another process holds the file lock: fail at once, wait a fixed time, or run a custom callback. Can the application use that setting to control the reader connections that a multi-reader database pool opens? If so, point to where it is applied to them.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: No: for pool readers the user's busy setting is never applied. Database.setupBusyMode chooses configuration.readonlyBusyMode ?? configuration.busyMode for read-only connections, which looks as if busyMode reaches readers (Database.swift:580-584).

CRITICAL: DatabasePool.readerConfiguration sets readonly = true on the reader configuration and, because readonlyBusyMode is nil, assigns .timeout(10) to it, so every reader waits up to 10 seconds whatever busyMode says (DatabasePool.swift:114-143; also used for makeSnapshot at DatabasePool.swift:946-950).

readonlyBusyMode is an internal property with no public setter, so the application cannot override the 10-second reader wait; DatabaseSnapshotPool.configure does the same default (Configuration.swift:333-335; DatabaseSnapshotPool.swift:236-254).

The public Configuration.busyMode (default .immediateError) therefore governs only the writer connection of a pool and the connections of a DatabaseQueue (Configuration.swift:326-331; Database.swift:585-607).

probes.query: A site publishes, in its name-server data, key material that lets clients hide the destination site name inside the TLS greeting. The server later rotates that key and refuses the client's greeting. Starting from the name-server answer, trace how the key material reaches the TLS handshake, which platform code supplies corrected material after the refusal, and which checks can stop the second attempt. Name the file and component for each step.
expectedFacts: RouteSelector.dnsLookup copies the key material from the name-server service-metadata record into Route.echConfigList only for DIRECT (no proxy) routes; RouteSelector.nextRoutes then keeps only the routes that carry key material when any do, so there is no non-ECH fallback route.

ConnectPlan.connectTls passes route.echConfigList into Platform.configureTlsExtensions; only Android17SocketAdapter (Android SDK 37+) applies it with SSLSockets.setEchConfigList (an unparsable list is skipped), while the plain JVM platform ignores it.

CRITICAL: After an SSLException, ConnectPlan.nextConnectionSpec first asks Platform.echRetryPlan(exception); it gives up at once if this plan is already an ECH retry (only one ECH retry), and the production implementation Android10Platform.echRetryPlan returns a plan only on SDK 37+ for EchConfigMismatchException, built from the exception's public hostname and retry config list; the base Platform returns null.
EchRetryPlan.getOrNull returns null (no retry) when the public name cannot be canonicalised, is an IP address, or matches the invalid patterns (leading or trailing dot, numeric label).

CRITICAL: Before retrying, nextConnectionSpec verifies the retry plan's public name against the session certificate with route.address.hostnameVerifier and throws EchUntrustedException on failure; on success it returns a copy of the plan with a new Route carrying the retry config list (null means retry without ECH) and echRetryPlan set.

attemptAnotherConnection returns false only for EchUntrustedException, so FastFallbackExchangeFinder and SequentialExchangeFinder stop trying other plans and addresses; a successful retry plan is pushed with deferredPlans.addFirst and tried before other deferred plans.

probes.notes: VERIFICATION: RouteSelector.kt:184-193 (echRoutes filter, routesToTry), :253-258 (echConfigList only Proxy.Type.DIRECT); ConnectPlan.kt:354-361 (configureTlsExtensions with route.echConfigList), :214-217 (catch SSLException -> nextConnectionSpec), :501-541 (nextConnectionSpec: echRetryPlan!=null return null :507; Platform.get().echRetryPlan :509; hostnameVerifier.verify(publicName) :514-521 EchUntrustedException; copy(route=Route(...echConfigList=nextEchRetryPlan.configList)) :522-531); Android17SocketAdapter.kt:55-95 (setEchConfigList, InvalidEchDataException -> null); Android10Platform.kt:54-61 (adapter list), :93-102 (SDK_INT<37 / EchConfigMismatchException); Platform.kt:144 (default null); EchRetryPlan.kt:46-57 (getOrNull); RetryTlsHandshake.kt:31 (attemptAnotherConnection = e !is EchUntrustedException); FastFallbackExchangeFinder.kt:96,100-103; SequentialExchangeFinder.kt:46,57. CHEAPEST ROUTE (est. 8 steps): 1 grep 'hide site name / TLS greeting / key material' in comments -> ech/ dir or Dns.kt ServiceMetadata; 2 find who reads echConfigList -> RouteSelector; 3 follow Route.echConfigList to ConnectPlan.connectTls -> Platform.configureTlsExtensions (Platform.kt, then per-platform overrides: Jdk9Platform ignores, Android17SocketAdapter applies); 4 find where the retry begins: grep echRetryPlan -> ConnectPlan.nextConnectionSpec; 5 open Platform.echRetryPlan overrides -> Android10Platform (SDK 37 guard); 6 open EchRetryPlan.getOrNull; 7 grep EchUntrustedException -> RetryTlsHandshake.attemptAnotherConnection; 8 open both finders. probes.query: A name-resolution client that talks to a remote HTTPS resolver is set to send each lookup in the request body instead of in the address. The application's response cache still stores and reuses those answers. Explain how a body-carrying request can be stored at all, what the stored key is made of, and where on the call path the substitution happens.
expectedFacts: In DnsOverHttpsQuery.Factory.newQuery, when the post option is on, the request is built with url(dnsUrl), a POST body holding the encoded DNS message, and cacheUrlOverride set to dnsUrl plus query parameters hostname=<question name> and type=<question type>.
Request.cacheUrlOverride (set through Request.Builder.cacheUrlOverride and copied by newBuilder) carries the alternative key URL; by default such POST (and QUERY) requests are not cached.

CRITICAL: CacheInterceptor's private requestForCache returns, when an override is set and the method is GET/QUERY (HttpMethod.isCacheable) or POST, a copy rewritten to GET with url = the override and the override cleared; it is used both for the lookup (cache?.get(...requestForCache())) and for the store (cacheNetworkRequest passed to cache.put).

CRITICAL: Cache.put only stores requests whose method is GET (invalidating methods like POST remove the entry and return null, other methods return null) and Cache.key is the md5 hex of the URL string, so only the rewritten GET is stored, under the override URL (hostname and type parameters).

probes.query: A host has both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses and the first address tried hangs silently. Without waiting for the full connect time limit, the client ends up connected through another address. Trace what switches this behaviour on, how the addresses are ordered, how new attempts are staggered, and what becomes of the attempts that lost the race.
expectedFacts: The client option fastFallback (default true) is read in RealCall.enterNetworkInterceptorExchange, which picks FastFallbackExchangeFinder when it is on and SequentialExchangeFinder otherwise, and also passes it to RealRoutePlanner and on to RouteSelector.
RouteSelector.nextRoutes applies reorderForHappyEyeballs only when fastFallback is on (after the ECH-only filter); with it off the DNS order is kept.

reorderForHappyEyeballs (InetAddressOrder.kt) partitions routes into Inet6Address vs others and, when both groups are non-empty, interleaves them (IPv6 first, alternating); with fewer than 2 routes or only one family the list is unchanged.

CRITICAL: FastFallbackExchangeFinder.find starts a new background TCP connect attempt every 250 ms (connectDelayNanos) while none has succeeded, waiting on a results queue; the first successful attempt wins.

CRITICAL: When a winner connects, cancelInFlightConnects cancels every losing in-flight plan and appends each loser's plan.retry() (a fresh ConnectPlan for the same route) to routePlanner.deferredPlans with addLast, so those routes can be tried again later; deferred plans are consulted before new routes in RealRoutePlanner.plan.
Only the winning plan continues with connectTlsEtc (TLS and tunnel work) and handleSuccess, which puts the connection in the pool.

RealCall is created with forWebSocket = true, and getResponseWithInterceptorChain leaves out the client's network interceptors for such calls (application interceptors still run).

probes.query: After a low-level network failure on an ordinary call, the client sometimes tries again (re-sends, uses another address, or uses a weaker TLS setup) and sometimes gives up. List every check that makes it give up, name where each lives, and say what exactly triggers it.
expectedFacts: RetryAndFollowUpInterceptor.recover gives up when the application disabled retries (chain.retryOnConnectionFailure is false, from the client setting or a per-call override).
recover gives up when the request send has started (the failure is not a ConnectionShutdownException) and the request body is one-shot or the failure is a FileNotFoundException.

RetryAndFollowUpInterceptor.isRecoverable returns false for ProtocolException, for InterruptedIOException unless it is a SocketTimeoutException before the request send started, for an SSLHandshakeException caused by a CertificateException, and for SSLPeerUnverifiedException; everything else is recoverable.

CRITICAL: RealCall.retryAfterFailure requires exchange.hasFailure and RealRoutePlanner.hasNext(failed connection) to be true; hasNext is true only with deferred plans, a pending next route, a retry route recovered from the failed connection (routeFailureCount == 0, noNewExchanges set, and same host reusable), or routes left in the current selection or selector; otherwise no retry.

ConnectPlan.nextConnectionSpec offers no further TLS configuration when this plan is already an ECH retry, when retryOnConnectionFailure is false, or when attemptAnotherConnectionSpec(e) is false (ProtocolException, any InterruptedIOException including connect timeouts, SSLHandshakeException caused by CertificateException, SSLPeerUnverifiedException, and any non-SSL exception); only other SSLExceptions move to the next compatible ConnectionSpec.
attemptAnotherConnection returns false only for EchUntrustedException, which makes both exchange finders abort instead of trying further plans or IP addresses.

probes.query: Behind a forward proxy that demands a login, an HTTPS request first needs the proxy to open a pipe to the origin, in plain text, before any encryption starts. If the proxy answers that initial request with a demand for credentials, which code loops to answer it, what limits the number of rounds, and what happens if the proxy hangs up after the demand? The code base has a second place that answers a proxy's demand for credentials; name it and say why it is not the one used at this stage.
expectedFacts: ConnectPlan.createTunnel is the loop: it writes the tunnel request on the raw socket with Http1ExchangeCodec, reads the response, returns null on 200, and on 407 takes the next request from route.address.proxyAuthenticator.authenticate(route, response), throwing IOException (Failed to authenticate with proxy) if that returns null.

CRITICAL: If the 407 response says Connection: close, createTunnel returns the next request and ConnectPlan.connectTunnel closes the raw socket and returns a ConnectResult whose nextPlan is a copy with attempt + 1 and the new tunnel request (a fresh TCP connection); otherwise the loop answers the challenge on the same socket.

CRITICAL: The round limit is MAX_TUNNEL_ATTEMPTS = 21, counted in ConnectPlan.connectTunnel across reconnects (nextAttempt < 21); beyond it the connect fails with ProtocolException 'Too many tunnel connections attempted: 21'. Challenges answered on the same socket inside createTunnel's loop are not counted by this limit (that loop ends only on 200, an authenticator returning null, or another status).

The first tunnel request is built in RealRoutePlanner.createTunnelRequest with minimal headers, and the proxy authenticator may pre-authenticate it by receiving a fake 407 response (Preemptive Authenticate, challenge OkHttp-Preemptive); returning null keeps the request as is.

The other place is RetryAndFollowUpInterceptor.followUpRequest's 407 (HTTP_PROXY_AUTH) branch, which calls chain.proxyAuthenticator for a 407 that arrives as an ordinary response after an exchange (requests sent through the proxy without a tunnel); it is not used while the tunnel is set up.

probes.query: A server-side JVM (not Android, not a native image) runs a Java 8 build from before the release that added built-in application-protocol negotiation. The first-registered security provider is an old Conscrypt release older than the minimum the code accepts, and the boot class path carries no add-on library for application-protocol negotiation. Which platform-adaptation class does the client end up using, what does it do when a connection configures TLS extensions, and which HTTP protocol do calls end up using? Several platform-selection routines exist; say which one applies.
expectedFacts: Selection happens in the jvmMain PlatformRegistry.findPlatform (not the androidMain registry and not the GraalSvm substitution): it checks whether the first security provider is named Conscrypt, then BC, then OpenJSSE, and each is used only if its buildIfSupported is non-null, otherwise it falls through.
ConscryptPlatform.isSupported requires the Conscrypt classes and atLeastVersion(2, 1, 0), so an older Conscrypt is not used.

Jdk9Platform.isAvailable is true only if java.specification.version parses as an int >= 9, or, when it does not parse (1.8), if SSLSocket has the getApplicationProtocol method (added in 8u251/252); here it is false.
Jdk8WithJettyBootPlatform.buildIfSupported returns null on Java 9+ or when the org.eclipse.jetty.alpn.ALPN classes are not on the boot class path.

CRITICAL: findPlatform returns the base Platform() (the open class) as the last fallback; its configureTlsExtensions is an empty no-op and getSelectedProtocol returns null, so ConnectPlan.connectTls sets protocol to HTTP_1_1 (no h2 negotiation).

probes.query: A developer configures a periodic liveness probe on the client to detect dead peers. Which kinds of connections actually send probes, how does the setting travel to the code that sends them, and what does the client do when an answer has not arrived by the time the next probe is due?
expectedFacts: The setting (OkHttpClient.pingIntervalMillis) reaches connections through RealCall.enterNetworkInterceptorExchange -> RealRoutePlanner -> ConnectPlan -> RealConnection, whose startHttp2 passes it to Http2Connection.Builder.pingIntervalMillis; it is used only for HTTP/2 (and h2 prior knowledge) connections, never for HTTP/1.1 connections.

CRITICAL: Http2Connection's init block schedules a periodic task on the writer queue; at each tick, if intervalPongsReceived < intervalPingsSent it calls failConnection(null), which closes the connection with PROTOCOL_ERROR (shutdown, cancels all open streams, cancels the socket); otherwise it increments the sent count and writes an INTERVAL_PING.
Web sockets use a separate mechanism: OkHttpClient.newWebSocket passes pingIntervalMillis to RealWebSocket, whose initReaderAndWriter schedules writePingFrame on its task queue.

CRITICAL: In RealWebSocket.writePingFrame, if the previous ping is still unanswered (awaitingPong) the web socket fails with SocketTimeoutException ('sent ping but didn't receive pong within ...ms'), delivering listener.onFailure and cancelling the socket; onReadPong resets awaitingPong.
Web socket handshakes force HTTP/1.1 (ONLY_HTTP1), so the HTTP/2 ping task never runs for web sockets.

probes.query: An application interceptor swaps in a different pool of reusable connections for just one call. Which pool supplies and receives the connection that call uses, and which pool is told when the call ends and its connection becomes idle? Do these differ, and what is the consequence?
expectedFacts: RealInterceptorChain.withConnectionPool returns a chain copy with the override and is allowed only before an exchange exists (check(exchange == null)), so a network interceptor gets an IllegalStateException.

RealCall.enterNetworkInterceptorExchange builds the RealRoutePlanner with chain.connectionPool.delegate, so pooled-connection lookups (callAcquirePooledConnection) use the override pool, and ConnectPlan.handleSuccess puts a newly made connection into that same pool (connectionPool.put) which schedules its cleanup.

CRITICAL: RealCall keeps a private connectionPool field initialised once from client.connectionPool.delegate, and releaseConnectionNoEvents calls that field's connectionBecameIdle(connection) when the call's last use ends; so the idle notification goes to the client's own pool, not the override pool.

CRITICAL: Consequence: the client pool's connectionBecameIdle will, if the connection has noNewExchanges or the client pool's maxIdleConnections is 0, mark it noNewExchanges, try to remove it (a no-op there) and return true so RealCall closes the socket even though it lives in the override pool; otherwise it only schedules the client pool's cleanup and returns false. The override pool is never told and relies on its own cleanup task.

probes.query: Compare two clients: a plain one, and one with the optional Brotli support added as an ordinary application-level interceptor. A caller asks for a byte range of a large file from a server that compresses whenever it is allowed to. For each client, say what compression the request advertises, who decompresses the answer, and what the caller receives if the server replies with a compression scheme the add-on does not know.
expectedFacts: BrotliInterceptor is CompressionInterceptor(Brotli, Gzip), registered as an application interceptor, so it runs before BridgeInterceptor in RealCall's chain.
CompressionInterceptor.intercept adds Accept-Encoding 'br, gzip' whenever its algorithm list is non-empty and the request has no Accept-Encoding of its own; it does not look at a Range header.

BridgeInterceptor advertises gzip (and later gunzips) only when the request has neither an Accept-Encoding nor a Range header; the plain client therefore advertises no compression for a range request and delivers the body untouched.
CRITICAL: With the add-on, the header is already present when the request reaches BridgeInterceptor, so Bridge does no gzip handling and the add-on's decompress step handles both br and gzip.

CRITICAL: CompressionInterceptor.decompress acts only if response.promisesBody() and Content-Encoding matches (case-insensitively) a configured algorithm; it then strips Content-Encoding and Content-Length and returns a streaming body of unknown length; an unrecognised encoding (for example deflate) is returned unmodified with Content-Encoding intact, so the caller gets compressed bytes.
If the caller sets its own Accept-Encoding, the add-on passes the request through and Bridge also leaves it alone, so the caller receives the raw compressed response.

probes.query: When the name-server data for a site includes service-binding advice, meaning a different port to use, a list of supported application protocols, and hint addresses, does the client's connection planning act on that advice? If so, where; if not, say what exists and why it has no effect.
expectedFacts: What exists: DnsMessageReader parses the HTTPS record parameters (alpn, no-default-alpn, port, ipv4/ipv6 hints, ech) and StateMachineDnsCall builds Dns.Record.ServiceMetadata(alpnIds, port, ipAddressHints, echConfigList), whose KDoc describes how clients should use them.

CRITICAL: RouteSelector.dnsLookup consumes only ServiceMetadata.echConfigList (looked up by hostname and applied only on DIRECT routes); alpnIds, port and ipAddressHints are never read by connection planning (they appear only in the record class, its equals/hashCode/toString and the DNS message reader/writer).

probes.query: In which situations does the connection-pooling layer itself close a connection that it is tracking and then carry on, because that connection is broken, too old, idle for long and unresponsive, or because the thread that owned it is gone? Cover both the default behaviour and the optional add-ons; name each situation, its trigger, and what the pool does next. Do not count explicit user requests to disconnect.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: In hold, an exception that is a DatabaseDisconnectError or a driver error classified by disconnect_error? makes the pool disconnect the connection, drop its allocation and call fill_queue(1) (timed queue), then re-raise the error; the failed operation is not retried.

When the pool is full and a new connection is needed, try_make_new (timed queue) and assign_connection (threaded) find connections allocated to threads that are no longer alive, remove them and disconnect them, then make room (the timed queue also calls fill_queue(count) so waiting threads get connections).

CRITICAL: The connection_validator extension's acquire checks a connection that has been idle longer than the validation timeout (default 3600 seconds), runs valid_connection?, and if the check is false removes the allocation, disconnects it via disconnect_acquired_connection and redoes acquisition to get another.

The connection_expiration extension's acquire disconnects any connection older than its expiration time (default 14400 seconds plus a random delay, set when the connection is made) regardless of health, then redoes acquisition.

The transaction_connection_validator extension turns a disconnect error raised while beginning a transaction into a DisconnectRetry (a DatabaseDisconnectError), so hold discards that connection; Database#transaction then retries with a new connection (at most 5 attempts in total) unless the retry would get the same connection, and otherwise raises the original database error.

probes.query: In a SQLite table, a column declared with a date-time type holds, for some rows, a plain whole number (seconds since 1970) and, for others, a decimal number (a day count from an ancient epoch) instead of text. When a model loads such a row, which code picks the converter, which code turns the stored number into the application's time value, which time zone is assumed for the stored number, and where is the application time zone finally applied?
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: The SQLite dataset's fetch_rows picks, for each result column, the conversion proc registered for its declared type name (base_type_name lowercases and strips the parenthesised size) and applies it to every non-nil value.
SQLite::Database#adapter_initialize registers the database's to_application_timestamp method as the conversion proc for the 'datetime' and 'timestamp' declared types.

SQLite's to_application_timestamp override handles Integer by Time.at(n).to_s (Unix seconds, rendered with the local system offset) and Float by DateTime.jd(f).to_s (Julian day number, rendered at +00:00, i.e. UTC), passes String to super, and raises Sequel::Error for other types.
The generic Database#to_application_timestamp (database/misc.rb) calls Sequel.convert_timestamp(value, timezone), where the database's timezone is its own setting or else Sequel.database_timezone.

CRITICAL: convert_input_timestamp parses the string with Sequel.string_to_datetime and, because the strings made from numbers carry an explicit offset (Date._parse has an :offset), does not reinterpret them in the database timezone; convert_timestamp then calls convert_output_timestamp with Sequel.application_timezone (:utc -> getutc, :local -> getlocal, nil -> unchanged).

probes.query: On the embedded single-file SQL database adapter, when application code takes an exclusive row lock on a record it has already loaded, inside a transaction, so that other writers must wait, does the library send any row-locking clause to the database? If something close exists, say what it does instead.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: SQLite's DatasetMethods#select_lock_sql is 'super unless @opts[:lock] == :update', so the FOR UPDATE lock style is silently omitted (the comment says this avoids raising errors for compatibility with other databases).
Model#lock! only calls _refresh on this.lock_style(style) (default :update), so on SQLite it reloads the row with a plain SELECT and takes no row lock.

The generic Dataset#select_lock_sql in dataset/sql.rb would append ' FOR UPDATE' for :update and appends a String lock style verbatim; the SQLite override suppresses only the :update symbol, so a raw string style would still be appended.

The nearest real concurrency control on SQLite is the transaction mode (begin_new_transaction uses opts[:mode] or the database's transaction mode: deferred, immediate or exclusive), which locks at database level, not per row.
